blocks.body:
Primes thin out. There are $25$ below $100$, $168$ below $1000$ and $78498$ below a million. From tables of this kind Gauss and Legendre guessed, in the 1790s, that near $x$ about one integer in $\log x$ is prime. The prime number theorem makes this precise: $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$.

The proof had to wait a century. In 1896 Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin, working independently, proved it using Riemann's zeta function, and the decisive input was that $\zeta(s)$ has no zeros on the line $\operatorname{Re}s=1$. This lesson explains why that is the key point, proves it, and outlines the rest of the argument.

blocks.title: Three equivalent forms
blocks.body:
The theorem can be stated with any of the counting functions from [[chebyshev]]:
$$\pi(x)\sim\frac{x}{\log x}\iff \theta(x)\sim x\iff\psi(x)\sim x .$$
Here $\theta(x)=\sum_{p\le x}\log p$ and $\psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)$. The equivalences are elementary. $\psi-\theta$ only involves prime powers and is $O(\sqrt x\log x)$. Passing between $\pi$ and $\theta$ is partial summation with weight $\log p$. Analysts prefer $\psi$, because its Dirichlet series is exactly $-\zeta'/\zeta$.

A better approximation than $x/\log x$ is the logarithmic integral
$$\operatorname{li}(x) = \int_2^x\frac{dt}{\log t} = \frac{x}{\log x}-\frac{2}{\log2}+\int_2^x\frac{dt}{\log^2t}.$$
The last integral is $O(x/\log^2x)$, so $\operatorname{li}(x)\sim x/\log x$, and $\pi(x)\sim\operatorname{li}(x)$ is the same theorem. A notational warning: many books write $\operatorname{Li}(x)$ for this integral from $2$ and reserve $\operatorname{li}(x)$ for the principal-value integral from $0$. The two differ by the constant $1.045\ldots$, which is irrelevant here.

blocks.title: Why zeta knows about primes
blocks.body:
For $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ the Euler product $\zeta(s)=\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ ([[zeta]]) can be differentiated logarithmically:
$$-\frac{\zeta'(s)}{\zeta(s)}=\sum_p\frac{\log p\;p^{-s}}{1-p^{-s}}=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^s}.$$
By [[mellin]] (Perron's formula), $\psi(x)$ can be recovered from this Dirichlet series as a contour integral, and its size is governed by the poles of $-\zeta'/\zeta$.

The pole of $\zeta$ at $s=1$ gives $-\zeta'/\zeta$ a simple pole with residue $+1$, and this produces the main term $x$. A zero $\rho$ of $\zeta$ gives $-\zeta'/\zeta$ a pole with residue $-1$ (times the multiplicity), and this produces a term $-x^\rho/\rho$, of absolute value $x^{\operatorname{Re}\rho}/|\rho|$. That is the content of the [[explicit-formula]].

So if $\zeta(1+it)=0$ for some $t$, there would be a term of size comparable to $x$ that oscillates like $x^{it}$, and $\psi(x)\sim x$ would fail. Ruling out zeros on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ is the heart of the matter.

blocks.title: Non-vanishing on the line Re s = 1
Proof (the 3–4–1 argument)
blocks.body:
Let $s=\sigma+it$ with $\sigma>1$. Taking logarithms of the Euler product and real parts,
$$\log|\zeta(\sigma+it)| = \sum_p\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\cos(kt\log p)}{k\,p^{k\sigma}}.$$
For every real $\theta$ we have $3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta = 2(1+\cos\theta)^2\ge0$. Apply this with $\theta=kt\log p$, multiply by the positive weight $1/(kp^{k\sigma})$ and sum:
$$3\log|\zeta(\sigma)|+4\log|\zeta(\sigma+it)|+\log|\zeta(\sigma+2it)|\ge0,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \big|\zeta(\sigma)^3\zeta(\sigma+it)^4\zeta(\sigma+2it)\big|\ge1 .$$
Now suppose $\zeta(1+it_0)=0$ with $t_0\ne0$, and let $\sigma\to1^+$. Then:
- $\zeta(\sigma)\le \sigma/(\sigma-1)$, so $\zeta(\sigma)^3=O((\sigma-1)^{-3})$;
- $\zeta$ is holomorphic near $1+it_0$ and vanishes there, so $|\zeta(\sigma+it_0)|\le C(\sigma-1)$ and the fourth power is $O((\sigma-1)^4)$;
- $\zeta$ is holomorphic at $1+2it_0$ (this is where $t_0\ne0$ is used, since the only pole is at $s=1$), so $\zeta(\sigma+2it_0)$ stays bounded.

The product is therefore $O(\sigma-1)\to0$, contradicting the inequality. Hence $\zeta(1+it_0)\ne0$.

blocks.title: From non-vanishing to the asymptotic
blocks.body:
Turning "no zeros on $\operatorname{Re}s=1$" into "$\psi(x)\sim x$" requires a Tauberian theorem. A short route is due to D. J. Newman (1980), as streamlined by D. Zagier (1997). Let $\Phi(s)=\sum_p\log p\,p^{-s}$.

1. $\Phi(s)-\frac1{s-1}$ extends holomorphically to a neighbourhood of the closed half-plane $\operatorname{Re}s\ge1$. Indeed $-\zeta'/\zeta(s)=\Phi(s)+\sum_p\frac{\log p}{p^s(p^s-1)}$. The last sum is holomorphic for $\operatorname{Re}s>\frac12$. And $-\zeta'/\zeta(s)-\frac1{s-1}$ is holomorphic on $\operatorname{Re}s\ge1$, because the pole at $1$ is simple and, by the theorem, there are no zeros.

2. Chebyshev's bound $\theta(x)=O(x)$ makes $f(t)=\theta(e^t)e^{-t}-1$ bounded on $t\ge0$. For $\operatorname{Re}z>0$ a change of variables gives
$$\int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-zt}\,dt=\frac{\Phi(z+1)}{z+1}-\frac1z,$$
and by step 1 the right side is holomorphic on $\operatorname{Re}z\ge0$.

3. Newman's analytic theorem: if $f$ is bounded and locally integrable on $[0,\infty)$ and its Laplace transform extends holomorphically to $\operatorname{Re}z\ge0$, then $\int_0^\infty f(t)\,dt$ converges. (The proof is about a page of contour integration with [[residues]]-type estimates; we omit it.) Hence $\int_1^\infty\frac{\theta(x)-x}{x^2}\,dx$ converges.

4. Convergence of that integral forces $\theta(x)\sim x$. Suppose $\theta(x)\ge\lambda x$ for some fixed $\lambda>1$ and arbitrarily large $x$. Since $\theta$ is nondecreasing,
$$\int_x^{\lambda x}\frac{\theta(t)-t}{t^2}\,dt\ \ge\ \int_x^{\lambda x}\frac{\lambda x-t}{t^2}\,dt=\int_1^\lambda\frac{\lambda-u}{u^2}\,du>0,$$
a fixed positive amount over intervals going off to infinity. That contradicts the Cauchy criterion for the convergent integral. The case $\theta(x)\le\lambda x$ with $\lambda<1$ is symmetric, using $[\lambda x,x]$. So $\theta(x)/x\to1$.

blocks.title: How good is the approximation?
The numbers
blocks.solution:
With $\operatorname{li}(x)=\int_2^x dt/\log t$:

- $x=10^6$: $\pi=78498$, $x/\log x\approx72382$, $\operatorname{li}\approx78626.5$; ratios $\pi/(x/\log x)=1.0845$, $\pi/\operatorname{li}=0.99837$.
- $x=10^7$: $\pi=664579$, $x/\log x\approx620421$, $\operatorname{li}\approx664917.4$; ratios $1.0712$ and $0.99949$.
- $x=10^8$: $\pi=5761455$, $x/\log x\approx5428681$, $\operatorname{li}\approx5762208.3$; ratios $1.0613$ and $0.99987$.
- $x=10^9$: $\pi=50847534$, $x/\log x\approx48254942$, $\operatorname{li}\approx50849233.9$; ratios $1.0537$ and $0.99997$.

Two lessons. First, $x/\log x$ approaches $\pi(x)$ very slowly from below. Since $\pi(x)\approx\operatorname{li}(x)$ and, by integration by parts, $\operatorname{li}(x)/(x/\log x)=1+1/\log x+\cdots$, the ratio exceeds $1$ by roughly $1/\log x$, and $1/\log 10^9\approx0.048$. Second, $\operatorname{li}(x)$ is far better: the absolute error $\operatorname{li}(x)-\pi(x)$ is only about $1700$ at $10^9$, smaller than $\sqrt x\approx31623$. In fact $\pi(x)<\operatorname{li}(x)$ for every $x$ from $8$ to $10^6$, and much further. Littlewood's theorem shows this pattern must eventually break.

blocks.title: The n-th prime
blocks.body: Show that the prime number theorem is equivalent to $p_n\sim n\log n$, where $p_n$ is the $n$-th prime. How accurate is this at $n=10^6$?
blocks.solution:
Assume $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$. Since $\pi(p_n)=n$, we get $n\sim p_n/\log p_n$. Taking logarithms, $\log n=\log p_n-\log\log p_n+o(1)$, so $\log n\sim\log p_n$. Hence $p_n\sim n\log p_n\sim n\log n$.

Conversely, assume $p_n\sim n\log n$. Then $p_{n+1}/p_n\to1$. Given $x$, let $n=\pi(x)$, so $p_n\le x<p_{n+1}$ and $x\sim p_n\sim n\log n$. Then $\log x\sim\log n$, and $n\sim x/\log n\sim x/\log x$.

Numerically $p_{10^6}=15485863$, while $n\log n\approx13815511$, a ratio of $1.121$. A sharper version of the same argument gives $p_n=n(\log n+\log\log n-1+o(1))$. This yields $15441302$, within $0.3\%$.

blocks.title: Ratios of primes are dense
blocks.body: Using the prime number theorem, show that (a) for every $\varepsilon>0$ the interval $(x,(1+\varepsilon)x]$ contains a prime for all large $x$; (b) the set $\{p/q: p,q\text{ prime}\}$ is dense in $(0,\infty)$.
blocks.solution:
(a) We have $\pi((1+\varepsilon)x)-\pi(x) = \frac{(1+\varepsilon)x}{\log((1+\varepsilon)x)}-\frac{x}{\log x}+o\Big(\frac{x}{\log x}\Big)$. Since $\log((1+\varepsilon)x)\sim\log x$, this equals $\frac{\varepsilon x}{\log x}(1+o(1))$, which tends to infinity. (Chebyshev's bounds alone give this only for $\varepsilon$ large, such as Bertrand's $\varepsilon=1$.)

(b) Let $0<a<b$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ with $(1+\varepsilon)a<b$. By (a) there is $X$ such that every $x>X$ has a prime in $(x,(1+\varepsilon)x]$. Take any prime $q>X/a$ and apply this with $x=aq$. We get a prime $p$ with $aq<p\le(1+\varepsilon)aq<bq$, so $a<p/q<b$.

blocks.body:
- $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$ is a statement about the ratio. The difference $\pi(x)-x/\log x$ is about $x/\log^2x$ and tends to infinity.
- The theorem says nothing about short intervals such as $(x,x+\sqrt x]$, or about gaps between consecutive primes beyond their average size $\log p$. See [[prime-patterns]].
- In the proof of $\zeta(1+it)\ne0$ the condition $t\ne0$ is essential. At $t=0$ the factor $\zeta(\sigma+2it)$ is the pole itself.
- The inequality $|\zeta^3(\sigma)\zeta^4(\sigma+it)\zeta(\sigma+2it)|\ge1$ holds only for $\sigma>1$, where the Euler product converges.
- Check whether a book's $\operatorname{li}$ starts at $0$ or at $2$ before comparing numbers.

Quantifying the key step, so that there are no zeros not just on but near $\operatorname{Re}s=1$, gives error terms. This is the subject of [[zero-free-region]], and the bridge between zeros and primes is the [[explicit-formula]]. Replacing $\zeta$ by Dirichlet $L$-functions gives the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions ([[l-functions]], [[siegel-walfisz]]). The heuristic "a random $n$ near $x$ is prime with probability $1/\log x$" underlies Cramér's model and the conjectures in [[prime-patterns]] and [[probabilistic-nt]]. The best possible error term is the [[rh]].

1. Integrate by parts twice to show $\operatorname{li}(x)=\frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\log^2x}+O\Big(\frac{x}{\log^3x}\Big)$.
2. Show that the prime number theorem implies $p_{n+1}/p_n\to1$, and that the number of primes in $(x,2x]$ is asymptotic to $x/\log x$.
3. (Chebyshev) Suppose only that $\lim_{x\to\infty}\pi(x)\log x/x=c$ exists. Using Mertens' estimate $\sum_{p\le x}1/p=\log\log x+O(1)$ from [[mertens]], show that $c=1$.
4. Show that $\psi(x)-\theta(x)=O(\sqrt x\log x)$, and deduce $\theta(x)\sim x\iff\psi(x)\sim x$.
